title: NIST AI RMF Generative AI Profile July 2026 — What It Changes for Federal AI Procurement
context: 2026-08-14 engine cycle — NIST published the Generative AI Profile (AI 600-1) as a cross-sector companion to the AI RMF 1.0, creating new measurement expectations for federal procurement starting in FY2027
body: NIST released the AI RMF Generative AI Profile in July 2026 as the long-awaited crosswalk that maps the original voluntary AI Risk Management Framework onto the specific failure modes of generative AI systems. The Profile is not a new framework — it layers GenAI-specific risks onto the existing Govern-Map-Measure-Manage structure. For federal procurement, this changes the game: agencies issuing AI-related RFPs in FY2027 are expected to reference the Profile, and the Federal Acquisition Regulatory Council has signalled that OSCAL-formatted measurement evidence — including GenAI-specific axes — will be the preferred submission format for contractor AI risk assessments under the FedRAMP OSCAL September 30 mandate. The Profile identifies twelve GenAI-specific risk categories, including: confabulation risk (hallucination measurement), prompt-injection susceptibility, jailbreak resilience, data-memorisation leakage, bias amplification across demographic slices, refusal-behaviour consistency, content provenance, model-inversion risks, energy-cost transparency, chain-of-thought faithfulness, sandbox-escape attempts, and downstream harm propagation. For a verification-first operator supplying AI systems to the federal government, the Profile is an answer-first opportunity: pre-signed measurement evidence across all twelve GenAI axes, formatted in OSCAL and delivered with a verified measurement credential, satisfies the Profile Map and Measure functions in a single submission. The Council of AI positions the NIST GenAI Profile as the most important AI procurement document of 2026 — it transforms the RMF from a voluntary guide into a de facto procurement requirement for anyone selling AI to the US federal government. The question is no longer whether you have an AI governance policy; it is whether you have signed, per-model, per-axis measurement evidence that an auditor can verify in under sixty seconds.
